main_damage_causes: Fred and George are consistently treated as a single interchangeable unit in the film corpus, erasing Fred's slightly more dominant comic voice and individual initiative that the books establish.

The removal of Fred and George's compartment visit on the Hogwarts Express eliminates the scene that personally establishes Fred's warm, proactive relationship with Harry — a relationship that is important throughout the saga.
Fred's individual lines and beats are frequently reassigned to George or delivered jointly, meaning Fred has almost no solo characterisation in the available film corpus.
Systematic removal of Fred's dialogue and individual agency in ensemble scenes, collapsing him into the background of group shots rather than letting him function as a distinct voice

Loss of the conversational and analytical Fred — particularly the Dobby discussion and the post-brawl Lockhart observation — which means the film never establishes that Fred is intelligent and politically aware, only that he is comedic

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Platform 9¾ twin swap prank
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Fred initiates the twin-swap gag with clear comic confidence: 'I'm not Fred, I'm George... Honestly, woman, you call yourself our mother? Can't you tell I'm George?' before revealing 'Only joking, I am Fred.' The humour is sharp and self-assured, with Fred driving the joke.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film the lines are redistributed: George says 'He's not Fred, I am!' and Fred delivers 'Honestly, woman, you call yourself our mother.' The joke lands but the attribution of who initiates and who delivers the punchline is swapped/muddled compared to the book, slightly diffusing Fred's individual comic voice.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A minor redistribution of lines between the twins that slightly flattens Fred's individual initiative in the gag. Because the twins are so frequently interchangeable in the films, this begins a pattern of erasing Fred's slightly more dominant comic role, but in isolation the damage is small.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 — Quidditch Seeker announcement, Fred and George's reaction
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book gives Fred and George distinct, individual voices in this moment. Fred says 'Well done' quietly and knowledgeably ('Wood was almost skipping when he told us'), and then both twins express genuine team pride and confidence, before departing to find Lee Jordan's secret passageway — showing their social energy and independent agency.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, George delivers the lines about their Beater role ('Our job is to make sure that you don't get bloodied up too bad') and the dark Quidditch humour ('But no one's died in years. Someone will vanish occasionally... but they'll turn up in a month or two!'). Fred's only attributed line is 'Brutal.' Fred is reduced to a one-word response while George carries the scene's characterisation.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Fred's book characterisation includes warm team pride and confident, independent humour. In the film this beat is almost entirely handed to George, making Fred a near-silent presence and beginning the pattern of the twins being treated as one interchangeable unit rather than two distinct personalities.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 — Sorting Hat arrival, 'We got Potter!'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book does not feature a moment where Fred and George shout out about Harry's sorting. Their relationship with Harry at this stage is warm but not yet loudly proprietorial — they help him at the station and greet him on the train, but their Sorting Hall behaviour is not described as an outburst.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Fred and George shout together 'We got Potter! We got Potter!' when Harry is sorted into Gryffindor. This is a film-only invention that presents them as an indistinct chanting unit rather than individuals.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While not severely damaging, the moment reinforces the film's tendency to fuse the twins into one undifferentiated comic chorus rather than two characters. Fred specifically loses any individual beat here.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 — Train scene, Fred's absence from compartment introduction
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Fred and George return to Ron's compartment specifically to introduce themselves to Harry by name: 'Fred and George Weasley. And this is Ron, our brother.' This is a warm, socially confident moment establishing Fred and George as individuals who take initiative in welcoming Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's train scene (Scene 2) shows no visit by Fred and George to Harry and Ron's compartment. The introduction of Fred and George as individuals — and their warm, proactive welcome of Harry — is entirely absent. George's only mention in the train scene is Ron referencing that 'George swore he got a bogey-flavoured one once,' reducing him (and Fred) to off-screen background figures.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's compartment visit is the foundation of Fred and George's relationship with Harry: it shows them as warm, individually named, socially confident people who seek Harry out. Removing it means the film never establishes Fred as someone who personally initiates a connection with Harry, weakening the basis of their friendship and Fred's role as an early welcoming figure in the Weasley family dynamic.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Rescue from Privet Drive (Film Scene 1/13A-17)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Fred takes an active leadership role throughout the rescue: he drives the car, gives Harry instructions ('Tie that around the bars'), reassures Harry ('Don't worry, and stand back'), coordinates the trunk extraction ('A bit more... One good push'), and is the one physically pulling from inside the car. George picks the lock with a hairpin and both twins climb through the window. Fred and George together demonstrate competence, wit, and casual Muggle knowledge ('A lot of wizards think it's a waste of time, knowing this sort of Muggle trick'). Fred is clearly the driver and tactical lead.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film compresses the rescue so that Ron is the dominant speaking presence from the car window. Fred is established as driver visually but is given no dialogue during the actual rescue operation. The lock-picking, the trunk-heaving coordination, the reassuring lines, and the witty commentary on Muggle skills are entirely absent. Fred is a silent background figure. The non-theatrical exclusion of the 'Ford Anglia takes off' scene further strips the opening of the journey.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The rescue sequence is the first significant Fred Weasley characterisation moment in the saga. The book uses it to establish Fred as resourceful, confident, technically capable, and humorous under pressure. Stripping his dialogue and coordination role reduces him to a prop (the driver's seat) rather than an active, characterised participant. The Muggle-skills remark is a small but telling character beat that foreshadows his entrepreneurial, rule-bending creativity. Its loss means the film never establishes this dimension of Fred at all.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Arrival at the Burrow / Mrs. Weasley's scolding (Film Scene 2/18-19)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Fred's responses under Mrs. Weasley's fury are characteristically unrepentant and witty: 'It was cloudy, Mum!' and the muttered 'Perfect Percy.' He catches his mother's eye and bends over his plate without another word when talking about Ginny's crush, showing he knows exactly how far to push. He also volunteers the observation that Lockhart 'was asking that bloke from the Daily Prophet if he'd be able to work the fight into his report' — a sharp, observant aside. Throughout the scolding scene Fred cowers physically but maintains his irreverent voice.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's Burrow arrival compresses the scolding to a brief exchange dominated by Mrs. Weasley and Ron. Fred has no individual lines during the dressing-down. The 'It was cloudy, Mum!' comeback, the 'Perfect Percy' mutter, and the Lockhart observation are all absent. Fred is present but undifferentiated from the group.
damaging_scenes.explanation: These small reactive lines collectively define Fred's voice: he presses back against authority with humour even when cowed, and he notices things others miss. Losing them means the film establishes no individual personality for Fred in his home environment. The 'Perfect Percy' line is also a small but meaningful beat in the Fred-Percy sibling dynamic.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Flourish and Blotts brawl (Film Scene 2/30)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, when Malfoy insults the Weasleys, Fred and George immediately try to physically attack Malfoy ('Flint had to dive in front of Malfoy to stop Fred and George jumping on him'). There is also a yell of 'Get him, Dad!' from Fred or George during Mr. Weasley's charge at Lucius. After the scene, Fred volunteers the sharp observation about Lockhart using the brawl for publicity. These moments show Fred's fierce protective loyalty and his quick-eyed, sardonic reading of situations.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Fred and George fly for Draco's throat when Malfoy says 'Mudblood' and Oliver Wood holds them back. This is present in the film corpus. However, the 'Get him, Dad!' moment is absent, the post-brawl Lockhart-publicity observation is absent, and the physical charge at Malfoy is redirected to the Quidditch courtyard scene rather than the bookshop. The film does preserve the reactive lunge, so this is partial.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The post-brawl Lockhart observation is a small but characteristic Fred moment — he is the one who cuts through the chaos to notice the absurd cynicism of Lockhart's self-promotion. Its absence is a minor loss of his sardonic, observant voice, though the protective lunge at Malfoy is preserved in the film.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Dobby/warning discussion on the drive to the Burrow (book only — absent from film)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, during the car journey back to the Burrow, Fred engages substantively with Harry's account of Dobby. He offers the analytical theory that Dobby was 'sent to stop you coming back to Hogwarts' and that house-elves can't use magic without their master's permission. He speculates about the Malfoys' likely ownership of a house-elf. He cranes around to look at Harry while making his point about Lucius Malfoy being 'right in You-Know-Who's inner circle.' This is Fred operating as an intelligent, politically aware participant in the conversation — not just comic relief.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This entire conversation is absent from the film. The car journey to the Burrow is not depicted as a dialogue scene at all. The film moves directly from the rescue to the Burrow arrival.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the only moment in the book corpus where Fred demonstrates genuine analytical intelligence and political awareness about the wizarding world. His theory about Dobby is correct and shows he thinks critically. The film's complete omission of this conversation means Fred's intellectual dimension — distinct from George's and from the purely comedic register — is never established. It also removes a moment of Fred engaging seriously with Harry as an equal, which matters for their relationship.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Heir of Slytherin mockery scene (Film Scene 4/78 — partially excluded)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Fred and George march ahead of Harry in the corridors shouting 'Make way for the Heir of Slytherin, seriously evil wizard coming through!' This is explicitly framed as protective humour: 'Harry didn't mind; it made him feel better that Fred and George, at least, thought the idea of his being Slytherin's heir was quite ludicrous.' Fred also asks Harry loudly 'who he was planning to attack next' and George pretends to ward Harry off with a garlic clove. The scene runs over multiple days and shows the twins actively working to shield Harry's morale and social standing through comedy.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Per the non-theatrical exclusion rules, the 'Fred and George mock Harry' scene is cut from the theatrical release. In the film corpus (Scene 4/78), Fred's single line 'Make way for the Heir of Slytherin! Seriously evil wizard coming through!' appears, but the framing context — Harry finding comfort in it, the extended campaign of jokes, George's garlic bit — is absent. The excluded scene is precisely the one that contextualises this as protective loyalty rather than mere jest.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book makes explicit that Fred and George's mockery is a form of care: they are the only ones treating the accusation as obviously absurd, and Harry takes comfort specifically from their stance. Without the framing of the excluded scene, the single surviving line in the film reads as ambiguous at best — Ron's 'Fred's just having a laugh' and Harry's pained 'He's the only one' in the film actually frames Fred's joke as somewhat hurtful rather than supportive. This inverts the book's characterisation of Fred as emotionally protective toward Harry, damaging the Fred-Harry relationship dynamic.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Quidditch match / Rogue Bludger (Film Scene 4/65)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Fred and George work together actively and intelligently during the rogue Bludger crisis: Fred bats it away ('Gotcha!' he yelled), both twins fly flanking Harry, Fred diagnoses the tampering aloud ('Someone's tampered with this Bludger'), George tries to signal Wood for a time-out, George argues the case to Wood at the time-out ('We were twenty feet above her, stopping the other Bludger from murdering Harry'), and Fred responds to Harry's request to leave him alone with protective concern ('Don't be thick. It'll take your head off'). They are active, vocal, competent Beaters making tactical decisions.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, George shouts the warning ('Harry! Watch out!') and bats the Bludger away once. The time-out, the twins' tactical conversation with Wood, the verbal diagnosis of tampering, and Fred's 'Don't be thick' protective line are all absent. The Bludger subplot is compressed and the twins' agency within it is reduced to a single reactive beat from George.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Quidditch match is the primary action sequence in the book corpus where Fred demonstrates Beater competence, tactical thinking, and protective concern for Harry. The film reduces this to a single George moment, erasing Fred's specific contributions. The 'Don't be thick' line is a small but genuine expression of Fred's care for Harry. Losing the time-out sequence also removes the twins' role as Harry's active advocates within the team.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Ginny's worst day / Percy's girlfriend revelation on the train (Book Scene 219-228, film absent)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, on the train home Fred and George sit with Harry, Ron, Hermione, and Ginny. When Ginny reveals Percy has a girlfriend, 'Fred dropped a stack of books on George's head' — a physical comedy reaction of delight. Fred says 'Wouldn't dream of it' about teasing Percy while 'looking like his birthday had come early,' establishing his impish delight in information as currency. Earlier, on Ginny's worst day after the Chamber attack, Fred and George try to cheer Ginny up by covering themselves in fur and jumping out at her from behind statues — stopped only by Percy's threat to write to Mrs. Weasley.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Neither the train scene nor the twins' attempt to cheer Ginny up appears in the film corpus. These scenes are simply absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Percy's-girlfriend reveal is a small but vivid character beat: Fred's delight at having ammunition against Percy is perfectly in character, and the physical comedy of dropping books on George's head is the kind of spontaneous twin dynamic the film otherwise has little space for. The attempt to cheer Ginny up, though misguided, shows Fred's instinct to respond to distress with action and humour — a trait central to his character. Their absence leaves the film's Fred with very little to do in the second half of the story.

damaging_scenes.scene: Chamber of Secrets - Filibuster fireworks and salamander experiment (Book Scenes 183-184, film absent)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Fred rescues a salamander from a Care of Magical Creatures class and he and George feed it a Filibuster firework in the Gryffindor common room, causing it to shoot sparks and zoom around the room. This provokes Percy into 'bellowing himself hoarse.' The scene ends with Percy apoplectic and the salamander escaping into the fire with explosions. This is a characteristic Fred moment: experimental, rule-breaking, delighted in chaos, and specifically antagonising Percy.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene does not appear in the film corpus at all.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The salamander experiment is one of the clearest illustrations in the book corpus of Fred's defining trait: the fusion of genuine experimental curiosity with a delight in chaos and rule-breaking. It also develops the Fred-Percy antagonism as a comedic throughline. Its absence from the film leaves a gap in establishing what Fred actually does when left to his own devices.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 (Clock Tower Courtyard) - Marauder's Map handoff: activation by George instead of Fred
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book corpus (Scenes 79-103), Fred leads the entire Marauder's Map scene: Fred pulls it from his cloak 'with a flourish', Fred explains 'This, Harry, is the secret of our success', Fred recounts stealing it from Filch's office ('I whipped the drawer open, and grabbed -- this'), Fred gives the warning about saying 'Mischief managed.' The scene is driven by Fred's voice, theatricality, and initiative.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In Film Scene 5, George activates the map by saying 'I solemnly swear that I am up to no good' and touching his wand to the parchment. George also delivers the 'Moony, Wormtail, Padfoot and Prongs. We owe them so much' line. Fred's book-dominant role in this scene is redistributed to George.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Marauder's Map handoff is one of Fred's most characterful book moments — he orchestrates it theatrically, tells the origin story, and delivers the key lines. Shifting the activation and the reverential Marauders tribute to George dilutes Fred's individual agency and wit in a scene that is structurally his in the source material. It flattens the distinction between the twins at a moment designed to showcase Fred specifically.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 (Clock Tower Courtyard) - Marauder's Map handoff: origin story omitted
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 86-95 establish a full, comedic origin story: Fred and George as innocent first-years, the Dungbomb diversion, Fred physically stealing the map from Filch's drawer. Fred concludes: 'This little beauty's taught us more than all the teachers in this school.' This backstory reveals Fred's resourcefulness, daring, and pride in rule-breaking as a craft.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 6 reduces the origin to a single line from Fred: 'Nicked it from Filch's office, of course, first year.' No diversion, no comedic build-up, no sense of earned pride or ingenuity. The characterisation of Fred as a bold, clever mischief-maker with history and texture behind his pranks is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The origin story is not mere backstory — it is characterisation. It shows Fred's confidence, lateral thinking, and delight in recounting his own mischief. Reducing it to a throwaway line removes a key beat that distinguishes Fred as an active, inventive rulebreaker rather than simply a comic presence.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 (Hospital Wing) - Fred's bedside manner after Harry's fall
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 55-72 shows Fred at Harry's bedside displaying emotional range: he looks 'extremely white underneath the mud' (genuine fear), grabs Harry's shoulder and shakes it 'roughly' to pull him out of self-pity ('C'mon, Harry, you've never missed the Snitch before'), and later offers sincere encouragement: 'Don't beat yourself up, Harry, you're still the best Seeker we've ever had.' Fred is both bracing and warm, showing he genuinely cares about Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In Film Scene 4, Fred's hospital wing dialogue is reduced to 'Peaky? What d'you expect him to look like? He fell fifty feet' and 'Gave us a right good scare, mate.' The physical gesture of grabbing Harry's shoulder, the running Quidditch-points analysis, and the closing encouragement are all absent. Fred registers as a background quipper rather than someone emotionally invested.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book scene establishes that Fred's bond with Harry goes beyond comedy — he offers real comfort and practical reassurance. The film keeps only the quip and a brief acknowledgment of fear, losing the warmth and the demonstration that Fred and Harry share genuine mutual regard.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (Leaky Cauldron) - Fred's reunion with Harry: Leaky Cauldron banter replaces book greeting
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 7-13 show Fred greeting Harry with exaggerated mock-formality ('Simply splendid to see you, old boy'), then immediately pivoting to whispered mockery of Percy ('And last,' Fred muttered) and confiding the pyramid prank attempt to Harry. The sequence establishes Fred's irreverence, his specific targeting of Percy, and his easy intimacy with Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 2 replaces this with Fred joking about the Egypt photo ('George's nose looks positively massive in that photograph') and then riffing on his own nose. While comic, it is self-directed humour about a photograph, not the pointed Percy-mockery or the direct warm address to Harry that characterises the book reunion. Fred's affectionate, conspiratorial relationship with Harry at the reunion is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book reunion moment is a compact but telling piece of Fred-Harry relationship texture: Fred singles Harry out for a warm, theatrical greeting and immediately treats him as an insider for Percy jokes. The film substitutes generic twin banter that does not build Fred's individual bond with Harry.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 (Clock Tower Courtyard) - 'Mischief managed' instruction delivered by Fred after the scene, not as part of the handoff
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 102-103 has Fred deliver the 'Mischief managed' warning as part of the careful, responsible handoff — he is the one who ensures Harry knows how to protect the map. It is Fred's final word in the scene, combining his roguish persona with practical foresight.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In Film Scene 5-6, the 'Mischief managed' instruction is delivered by Fred as a parting aside ('Oh. And, Harry? When you're done, make sure to give it a tap and say, Mischief managed') after the main handoff scene has concluded and they are already leaving. It is structurally a throwaway rather than the capstone of a carefully orchestrated scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor but consistent with the pattern of flattening Fred's scene-ownership. In the book, this line closes the scene with Fred's characteristic mix of mischief and competence. In the film it is an afterthought, further reducing the sense that Fred has deliberately orchestrated this handoff.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 – Aging Potion / Age Line sequence
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Fred as the boldly confident, shrewd ringleader of the Age Line attempt. He reasons shrewdly that the impartial judge, not Dumbledore, decides the champion, so the Aging Potion only needs to fool the line. He steps forward with theatrical bravado, rocking on his toes 'like a diver preparing for a fifty-foot drop,' holding the crowd's attention deliberately. When ejected and bearded, he joins in laughing at himself and George, showing self-aware humor even in failure.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film condenses the attempt to a quick stunt shared equally between Fred and George with synchronized dialogue ('But that's why it's so brilliant. Because it's so pathetically dimwitted'). Fred's individual reasoning and the specific theatrical solo step-over are collapsed into a joint action. The shrewd logic Fred articulates in the book ('it's them we'll have to fool… Dumbledore's trying to stop us giving our names') is absent; the film makes it look like simple bravado rather than calculated, if flawed, reasoning.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Fred's defining trait of being the sharper, more analytically confident twin who leads and reasons aloud is lost. The film collapses his individual agency into a comedic double-act, reducing a character beat that distinguishes Fred from George into pure slapstick.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 – post-ejection bearded fight
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book explicitly states: 'Even Fred and George joined in [the laughter], once they had gotten to their feet and taken a good look at each other's beards.' Fred's self-deprecating humor and resilience in humiliation is a key character note.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Fred and George immediately start physically fighting each other after being ejected, bickering and wrestling while students chant 'Fight!' This replaces the books' shared laughter with petty squabbling.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Fred's capacity to laugh at himself even in failure is a core trait the book emphasizes. Replacing it with fraternal bickering misrepresents his good humor and resilience, and damages the warmth of the Fred-George dynamic, making them look foolish rather than charmingly self-aware.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Death Eater attack / camp evacuation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Fred acting with instinctive protectiveness: 'Fred, grabbing Ginny's hand and starting to pull her toward the wood.' Fred takes immediate, independent initiative to protect his younger sister without being told. The book also notes that Fred, George, and Ginny made it back safely while Bill, Charlie, and Percy sustained injuries.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Arthur explicitly delegates responsibility: 'Fred, George! Ginny is your responsibility. Go!' Fred and George's protective action is thus converted from independent character initiative into compliance with a direct parental order.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A small but meaningful loss: in the book Fred acts on his own moral instinct to protect Ginny; in the film he acts because his father told him to. This removes a beat of independent protective agency and reduces Fred to following instructions rather than demonstrating his own instincts.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 – post-first-task common room celebration, Fred and George's commentary on Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book has no equivalent scene where Fred comments on Harry's moral fiber in this way; the film invents specific dialogue here. However the book corpus does establish Fred's voice as someone who respects competence and daring, and who has a sharp, layered wit rather than simple teasing.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Fred says 'All that moral fiber, eh?' and later 'It's great' in a tone that reads as slightly dismissive or mocking toward Harry's second-place finish and the judges' reasoning. George echoes with 'Yeah, well done, Moral Fiber.'
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor voice issue: the film's Fred sounds slightly sardonic toward Harry's genuine heroism in a way that sits awkwardly against the book's Fred, who deeply respects Harry and by end of book gives him a heartfelt 'thanks' for the tournament winnings. The tone is not severely damaging but represents a slight misalignment of Fred's loyalty and warmth toward Harry.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 – second task betting with Fred and George taking bets from crowd
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus does not place Fred and George running a public betting operation at the second task. The book does establish their entrepreneurial nature and their earlier Quidditch World Cup bet with Bagman, but their presence at the second task in the book corpus is minimal and does not involve openly soliciting bets from students.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Fred and George are shown loudly running a betting stall ('Any bets? Any bets? Come on, place your bets! … Four go down. But do four come up?') including morbid odds on champion survival, with Ginny mildly rebuking them ('Don't be so mean').
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film introduces an invented scene that is broadly consistent with the twins' entrepreneurial character, so damage is low. However, the morbid framing ('do four come up?') about Harry specifically leans slightly against the book's portrayal of Fred's genuine warmth and loyalty toward Harry. It is a minor characterization drift rather than a severe distortion.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 – Fred passing note to Angelina / Yule Ball asking
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Fred asking Angelina with casual, direct confidence: he simply turns his head across the common room and shouts 'Oi! Angelina! Want to come to the ball with me?' without any prior note-passing or intermediary. The book presents this as a demonstration of Fred's easy social confidence — he hasn't even asked her yet when he tells Harry and Ron she's his date, then does it on the spot. He says 'piece of cake' afterward.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Fred is shown passing a written note to Angelina across the Transfiguration classroom ('GET A MOVE ON OR ALL THE GOOD ONES WILL HAVE GONE') — this note is actually addressed to Ron and Harry, and then Fred shouts 'Oi, Angelina?' and asks her. The core ask is preserved but the surrounding scene conflates the note-to-Ron with the ask itself, slightly muddying the clean spontaneity of the book moment.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minimal damage. The film does preserve Fred's confident, casual ask and Angelina's acceptance. The note conflation slightly reduces the pure spontaneous confidence of the book beat but does not meaningfully distort Fred's character.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Fred and George's arrival greeting at Grimmauld Place
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Fred and George arriving with distinct individual voices: Fred says 'You don't want to bottle up your anger like that, Harry, let it all out' and George says 'Hello, Harry, we thought we heard your dulcet tones.' Each twin has a separate, characterised line that shows their wit and warmth toward Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film the twins' greeting is collapsed: George says 'Thought we heard your dullest voices' and Fred says 'Don't bottle it up, though, mate. Let it out.' The lines are reassigned and compressed, flattening the distinction between the two characters into an interchangeable double act with no individual personality differentiation.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor but symptomatic: the book carefully gives each twin a distinct beat to establish them as individuals who happen to be twins, not a single comedic unit. The film immediately collapses them into one entity, beginning a pattern that persists throughout.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Fred and George's role in the Order briefing debate
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book gives Fred and George substantial spoken agency in the debate about whether they should be told Order information. They argue 'We're of age!' and Fred directly challenges Sirius ('Easy for you to say, stuck here! I don't see you risking your neck!'). They are vocal, principled, and emotionally invested — Fred reads the letter about Mr Weasley's condition, Fred half-rises from his chair waiting for news. Their adult status and emotional stakes in the Order are dramatised at length.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's Grimmauld Place briefing scene has the twins present but almost entirely silent. They contribute no spoken lines to the Order debate. Their 'of age' argument is absent. The confrontation between Fred and Sirius about risk and cowardice is completely cut. They are background dressing during the scene that defines their relationship to the Order and to the adult world.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This removes a defining moment of Fred's character: his willingness to challenge authority figures he respects (Sirius) when family is at stake, and his awareness of the hypocrisy of being told they are 'of age' but still excluded. It also removes the emotional complexity of Fred during the Mr Weasley vigil scenes. The loss hollows out their transition from comic relief to young adults with genuine stakes in the war.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 — Skiving Snackboxes demonstration reduced to a product pitch
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book gives an extended, vivid demonstration scene in the Gryffindor common room where Fred publicly vomits into a bucket, George follows, Lee Jordan Vanishes the vomit, and the twins take advance orders. Harry observes and reflects: 'You know, I don't get why Fred and George only got three OWLs each. They really know their stuff.' The scene establishes them as genuinely talented, entrepreneurially serious, and committed to their craft — they test products on themselves, they have worked on the formula all summer, they are building a real business.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In Film Scene 3, the Skiving Snackboxes are introduced as a brief comedic exchange: Fred says 'Sweets that make you ill,' George adds 'Get you out of class whenever you like,' Fred finishes 'Obtain hours of pleasure from unprofitable boredom.' This is a throwaway gag with no demonstration, no crowd, no business infrastructure shown, and no reflection on their talent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses the Snackbox demonstration to reframe Fred and George from pranksters into proto-entrepreneurs with genuine magical skill. Harry's admiring observation is the clearest signal to the audience that these characters deserve respect beyond comic relief. The film's reduction to a one-liner loses this reframing entirely.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 — Fred and George testing products on first-years
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has an extended scene where Fred and George give Fainting Fancies to first-years for pay, with clipboards and systematic observation. Hermione confronts them, Fred argues back ('We're paying them!', 'Course it is, they're alive, aren't they?'), and the scene shows their moral ambiguity — they genuinely believe they are being ethical (paid consent, antidote ready) while Hermione sees exploitation. Fred is 'thunderstruck' by Hermione's threat to write to their mother, showing where his real fear lies. This is a nuanced character scene.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This entire scene is absent from the film corpus. The first-year testing subplot, the confrontation with Hermione, and Fred's specific reaction to the threat about Mrs Weasley are all cut.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The absence removes the one scene in the book where Fred's ethical reasoning is examined — where his confidence meets a genuine moral challenge. It also removes a key data point showing that Fred's real vulnerability is his mother's disapproval, not authority figures. This makes him shallower.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3/4 — Ron prefect badge reaction
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book gives Fred an extended, layered reaction to Ron's prefect badge: initial disbelief ('There's been a mistake'), sarcasm ('No one in their right mind would make Ron a prefect'), then a pointed aside to Harry ('We thought you were a cert!'), followed by him clapping Harry on the back while giving Ron a scathing look, and making ongoing jokes through the scene ('Prefect... ickle Ronnie the Prefect'). This establishes Fred's genuine surprise that Harry wasn't chosen, and his competitive but affectionate relationship with Ron.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The prefect badge scene does not appear in the film corpus at all. There is no dramatisation of Fred's reaction to Ron's prefectship.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The prefect scene is important for Fred's relationship with both Ron (teasing sibling rivalry) and Harry (his genuine regard for Harry's standing). Its absence means the film never establishes Fred's specific dynamic with Ron beyond generic twin-brotherhood.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 — Fred and George's departure from Hogwarts
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book builds the departure across multiple scenes: the deliberate plan communicated to Harry, the swamp, being cornered by Umbridge, Fred's calm defiance ('Pretty amusing, yeah'), his statement 'I think we've outgrown full-time education', summoning their brooms with Accio, advertising Weasleys' Wizarding Wheezes to the assembled school, Fred telling Peeves 'Give her hell from us', and Peeves saluting. The departure is Fred's defining act of agency — planned, purposeful, generous (helping Harry access Umbridge's office), and triumphant.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Fred and George flying into the Great Hall on broomsticks throwing fireworks during an exam, with Umbridge reacting. The deliberate confrontation, Fred's spoken defiance of Umbridge, the Accio brooms moment, the advertising speech, and the Peeves instruction are all absent from the filmed version as shown in the corpus. The departure appears as spectacle rather than as a principled, planned act.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The departure is the climax of Fred and George's arc in Order of the Phoenix. The book version shows Fred as the architect of a principled rebellion — he has thought it through, communicated it to allies, used it to help Harry, and left with a specific instruction to Peeves that pays off later. The film version, based on the corpus, reduces it to a fireworks spectacle. The loss of Fred's spoken lines ('You know what? I don't think we are', 'Give her hell from us') removes his voice from his own defining moment.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Fred and George's magic at dinner ('whipping wands out')
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes Fred and George bewitching cauldrons and food to fly through the kitchen, causing near-injury to Sirius, and Fred apologising ('Sorry, Sirius, mate — didn't mean to'). This shows their carelessness with magic, their comfort with Sirius, and their genuine remorse when things go wrong.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Mrs Weasley scolding 'Just because you're allowed to use magic now does not mean you have to whip your wands out for everything!' after Fred and George do unspecified magic. The specific incident (bewitched cauldron nearly injuring Sirius, Fred's apology) is replaced with a generic scolding. Fred and George have no spoken lines or individual reaction in this beat.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor but consistent with the pattern: the book moment shows Fred as someone who is careless but genuinely remorseful and warm toward Sirius. The film genericises this into a background scolding, removing Fred's individual voice and his specific relationship with Sirius.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 — Fred and George as Dumbledore's Army members
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book shows Fred signing the DA parchment cheerfully and immediately, showing his commitment to the cause. He is vocal at the Hog's Head meeting, defending Harry against Zacharias Smith ('That's not what he said'), threatening Smith with his wand, and demonstrating real investment in Harry's leadership and the group's purpose.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's Hog's Head scene does not show Fred speaking or defending Harry against the sceptical boy. Fred and George are present in the pub scene but the corpus shows no spoken defence of Harry from Fred, no wand threat to the sceptic. In the DA training scenes, Fred and George appear briefly (the one-sickle bet on Hermione stunning George) but have no spoken lines that establish their individual commitment or relationship to Harry.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses the DA scenes to show Fred as one of Harry's most active and loyal defenders, willing to physically threaten someone who doubts Harry. The film reduces him to a background participant, losing the specific quality of his loyalty to Harry.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Night vigil after Mr Weasley's attack
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has Fred fall into a doze during the vigil, half-rise from his chair when Mrs Weasley enters, and then fall back into his chair with his hands over his face when she says Arthur will be all right. Fred pulls the letter about his father's condition from George's hands to read it himself. Fred is shown throughout as emotionally vulnerable, physically exhausted, and deeply loving toward his father — the comedy persona entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The night vigil and Mr Weasley's recovery scene at Grimmauld Place shows the family receiving the news, with a Christmas morning scene following. The specific physical and emotional beats attributed to Fred in the book — dozing, half-rising, falling back with hands over face — are not evidenced in the film corpus. Fred has no individual emotional moment in this sequence.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the book's primary scene showing Fred as a fully emotional person rather than a comedian. His physical collapse of relief when his father is confirmed safe is one of the few times the book strips away his performance. The film's failure to give Fred any individual emotional beat in this sequence means audiences never see beneath his comic surface, which diminishes the entire character.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 — Fred and George comforting injured Michael after DA
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: No book scene shows Fred and George treating an injured boy named Michael in this manner — this is a film-only beat.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In Film Scene 4, Fred and George tend to a boy named Michael whose hand has been hurt, with Fred saying 'Your hand's gonna be fine, Michael' and 'it's fading already.' This is a warm, caring moment that is not in the book corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is a rare case where the film adds something positive to Fred's characterisation not in the corpus — showing genuine care for a younger student. It does not damage the adaptation; it is noted only for completeness. No damage score applies, but it is included to flag that this invented beat is the exception rather than the rule in the film's treatment of Fred.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 - Weasleys' Wizard Wheezes shop floor, Fred & George on counter selling to the masses
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Fred giving Harry a personal tour, engaging him one-on-one with genuine warmth, shaking hands, noticing Hermione's bruise and immediately producing a remedy from his own pocket, explaining products with pride and detail (Patented Daydream Charms, Shield Hats, Decoy Detonators, Muggle magic tricks for Dad). Fred also firmly refuses Harry's money, citing the start-up loan with real emotional weight: 'You gave us our start-up loan, we haven't forgotten.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Fred and George are presented as a double act performing showmanship on a counter ('Step up! Step up!'), essentially interchangeable carnival barkers. The personal warmth toward Harry is reduced to a brief 'What'd you think, Harry?' / 'Amazing' exchange. The individual characterisation of Fred — his inventiveness, his entrepreneurial pride, his specific gratitude to Harry — is collapsed into a twin-act gimmick.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book carefully differentiates Fred from George even within their shared enterprise: Fred gives the personal tour, Fred notices Hermione's injury, Fred handles the emotional moment with Harry about the loan. The film renders both twins as a single undifferentiated unit, erasing Fred's individual voice and warmth.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 - Fred/George refusing Ron's money ('Ten Galleons') vs. Harry's free pass
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book shows Fred refusing Harry's payment with emotional sincerity ('You gave us our start-up loan, we haven't forgotten') while simultaneously charging Ron full price ('Three Galleons, nine Sickles') with affectionate but firm sibling teasing. The contrast reveals Fred's loyalty, fairness, and the specific debt of gratitude to Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film collapses the Ron pricing gag and the Harry free-pass moment into a single undifferentiated twin exchange: Ron asks the price, is told 'Five Galleons,' says he's their brother, and is told 'Ten Galleons.' Harry's specific exemption and the emotional reason behind it — the start-up loan — are completely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's scene establishes a meaningful emotional debt Fred and George owe Harry, which deepens their friendship and gives Harry's generosity in Book 4 retrospective weight. Removing it strips a key layer of Fred's loyalty and the Fred-Harry relationship of its grounding.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 - Wonder Witch / love potions / Ginny's boyfriends exchange
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book gives Fred the lead on the WonderWitch products reveal ('Follow me, ladies'), has him engage Ginny with a mix of teasing and genuine older-brother protectiveness, pressing her specifically about Dean Thomas and then about 'moving through boyfriends a bit fast' — showing Fred as attentive to family dynamics beneath the jokes. Ginny's Mrs. Weasley-ish glare is noted as something even Fred doesn't recoil from, hinting at mutual respect.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film the exchange is compressed: Fred mentions Dean Thomas briefly and Ginny dismisses it. The texture of Fred's protective teasing — the Pygmy Puffs interlude, the back-and-forth about multiple boys, Ginny's formidable glare — is largely lost. The moment reads as a quick gag rather than a characterised sibling dynamic.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Fred's protective but humorous older-brother role toward Ginny is part of his characterisation. The truncation reduces it to a throwaway line, weakening the sibling texture of the Weasley family dynamic.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 - Fred's individual presence vs. twin-unit presentation throughout the shop scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book consistently differentiates Fred and George even in the same scene: Fred gives the tour, George handles a customer, they tag in and out. Fred specifically says 'We're testing most of our products on ourselves' — showing personal investment and risk-taking. Fred's individual magenta robes are noted as clashing magnificently, marking him as a distinct personality.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film uses 'FRED/GEORGE' shared dialogue tags for multiple lines ('Step up! Step up!', 'Five Galleons', 'Ten Galleons', 'We've got eyes in the back of our heads'), presenting them as a single comedic unit with synchronised speech rather than two distinct individuals who happen to be twins.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Reducing Fred to half of a comedy double act erodes his individual agency, voice, and entrepreneurial identity. Over the course of the saga this matters because Fred's death needs to land as the loss of a specific, irreplaceable individual — damage here undermines that later payoff.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 & 7 - Burrow attack, Fred in the reeds
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The Burrow attack does not occur in the book at this point in the story. Book HBP has no scene where Fred participates in a defensive action against Bellatrix and Greyback at the Burrow. Fred's role in the book is domestic and comedic throughout HBP, with his serious side shown in the hospital visit to Ron and the shop's defence-product line — not in combat.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Fred (along with George, Ron, and Arthur) fans out through the burning reeds chasing Bellatrix and Greyback in a wholly invented action sequence. Fred is present but entirely non-speaking and functionally interchangeable with the other male Weasleys in the scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The invented scene neither harms nor develops Fred's characterisation — he is simply background bodies. Minor damage only because it uses screen time that could have developed Fred individually, and because placing Fred in a generic action role slightly dilutes his comedic-entrepreneur identity. Impact is low because he is not characterised here at all, just present.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 - Christmas at the Burrow, Fred filling cups
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Christmas scenes give Fred and George significant comedic and characterisation moments: the gnome-angel gag (Fred specifically catches the gnome that bit him and the gang stupefies and decorates it); Fred's sharp exchange about Percy ('Or he's the world's biggest prat'); the sprout-peeling scene where Fred refuses to help Ron with deliberate irony ('It's very character-building stuff'), and his announcement about the pretty girl in the village paper shop — all of which show Fred's wit, his layered feelings about Percy, and his individual spark.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 5 shows Fred and George filling cups with nog in the background while the scene focuses on Harry's conversation with Lupin and Tonks about Draco. Fred has no dialogue and no individual characterisation in this scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Christmas sequence is one of the richest sources of Fred's individual voice and his complex feelings about the family (especially Percy). The film reduces him to set dressing at a party, losing the Percy commentary, the gnome-angel business, and the sprout scene — all of which are defining Fred moments that cannot be recovered elsewhere in the film.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film — absence of Ron's poisoning hospital scene (Fred's investigative, serious side)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 137-156 shows Fred arriving at Ron's bedside (he and George arrive slightly late, having come from Hogsmeade), bringing a gift, and engaging in a sustained, serious analytical conversation about how Ron was poisoned. Fred asks 'How exactly did it happen?', speculates about Slughorn being a Death Eater, raises the possibility of the Imperius Curse, and drives the group's attempts to reason through the threat. This is one of the few moments where Fred's intelligence and genuine concern for family are foregrounded without comedy.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus contains no hospital scene involving Fred reasoning about Ron's poisoning. This material is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This scene is crucial for establishing that Fred is more than a joke-shop proprietor: he is perceptive, caring, and analytically sharp when family is in danger. Its absence means the film never shows Fred's serious register, leaving his character one-dimensional and making his eventual death in Deathly Hallows harder to feel as the loss of a complex person.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film — absence of Fred's Peruvian Instant Darkness Powder/Malfoy connection commentary
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 161: Ron says bitterly 'Fred and George's. I'm going to be having a word with them about who they let buy their products' — establishing that Fred and George's shop is implicated in enabling Malfoy's Death Eater operation, a morally complex detail that adds weight to the twins' entrepreneurial choices.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film does use the Peruvian Instant Darkness Powder (Harry picks it up in the shop and uses it on the train, Film Scene 2 and 4), but the later revelation that Malfoy used it to cover the Death Eaters' escape — and Ron's pointed comment about Fred and George's responsibility — is absent from the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book plants a subtle moral complexity around Fred and George's business: their products can be weaponised. Removing Ron's comment erases this nuance and lets the film use Fred's product for a fun Harry moment (train scene) without acknowledging the darker implication — a loss of thematic depth in Fred's characterisation.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (Polyjuice preparation, kitchen) — George delivers Fred's book line
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 5: Fred says 'Well, none of us really fancy it, Harry. Imagine if something went wrong and we were stuck as specky, scrawny gits forever.' Fred is the one with the sharp, self-deprecating wit here.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film script, the line 'Well, none of us really fancy it, mate' is given to Fred, but the follow-up joke about being 'scrawny, specky gits forever' is reassigned to George. The twins' individual voices are blurred, with George taking Fred's punchline.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Fred's wit and his specific comedic voice are diluted by giving his punchline to George. Minor but reflects a pattern of the film treating them as interchangeable rather than distinct individuals.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (Polyjuice preparation, kitchen) — Fred's 'goblin piss' quip exchange
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 5-7: Fred's humor is proactive and directed — he volunteers jokes ('Imagine if something went wrong'), teases Moody ('thirteen of us against one bloke'), and maintains a confident, irreverent tone throughout the scene. He is clearly the more verbally dominant twin.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 2: Fred's reactive quip to Moody ('Have a lot of experience with that, do you, Mad-Eye?') is present, but his broader pattern of leading the comedy — his line about 'thirteen of us against one bloke who's not allowed to use magic' and the extended banter about being 'better-looking' — is compressed or redistributed. The film Fred is reactive rather than proactive.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book establishes Fred as the sharper, more verbally dominant twin who drives comedy rather than merely reacts. The film compresses this into a single quip, flattening his distinct comedic agency in the scene.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 (Burrow sitting room, after George's injury) — Fred's emotional beat altered
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 37-44: Fred arrives pale and speechless, 'lost for words' for the first time Harry had known him — a rare crack in his persona. He gazes at George's wound 'as if he could not believe what he was seeing.' His relief-through-humor response ('Pathetic! With the whole wide world of ear-related humor before you, you go for holey?') is preceded by genuine terror ('What's wrong with him? Is his mind affected?'). The sequence shows Fred's vulnerability before his humor reasserts itself.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 5: Fred asks 'How do you feel, Georgie?' almost immediately upon entering, skipping the book's beat where Fred is described as stunned, pale, and genuinely lost for words. The film moves directly to the comedic exchange without the preceding moment of Fred's visible terror and speechlessness ('What's wrong with him? Is his mind affected?').
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's power in this scene comes from showing Fred — the eternal joker — rendered genuinely speechless and terrified before humor rescues him. This is one of the most revealing characterization moments for Fred in the entire series. Removing his terror strips the emotional depth from his subsequent joke and diminishes audience understanding of how much George means to him.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 (Burrow sitting room) — Fred's toast/leadership beat after Mad-Eye's death
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 49-54: Fred takes initiative in the grief scene — 'with a wave of his wand, he sent twelve full glasses soaring through the room to each of them' and leads the toast to Mad-Eye. Later he says 'Well said, Harry' unexpectedly after Harry's speech about trust, showing emotional and moral weight beneath the humor.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 5: The toast to Mad-Eye is absent from the film corpus. The scene ends with Fred nodding approvingly at George's ''Ear, 'ear' and saying 'Better' — a much smaller beat. Fred's proactive role in leading the group through grief (the wand-conjured glasses, the toast, the 'Well said, Harry') is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The toast scene is one of Fred's most important moments of group leadership and emotional maturity — he steps up when the room is in shock, uses magic to unify everyone, and later validates Harry in a way that is 'unexpected' even to Harry. Losing this removes a key demonstration that Fred is more than comic relief; he is a genuine leader and emotionally present member of the Order.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 12 (Spanning Bridge, Battle of Hogwarts) — Fred's battle presence reduced to a single line
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 160-161: Fred is shown actively commanding a 'small knot of students including Lee Jordan and Hannah Abbott,' with wands drawn, listening at a concealed passageway. He shouts 'Nice night for it!' as the castle quakes. He has a tactical role — defending a secret passageway — and is shown as a leader of a small unit.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 12: Fred and George 'burst out of the castle, grinning madly' and Fred delivers 'Nice night for it!' before Harry turns away to talk to Luna. There is no depiction of Fred commanding students or holding a defensive position; the moment is purely tonal/comedic.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Fred's tactical agency — leading a unit at a concealed passageway — is erased. His presence in the battle becomes decorative rather than functional, reducing him to a one-liner delivery before disappearing from the scene.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 15 (Battlements, Battle of Hogwarts) — Fred and George's battle role generalized
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 157: Fred specifically volunteers himself and George to 'organize defense of the entrances or the passageways into the school,' and Kingsley nods approval. This is a self-assigned, competence-driven role that reflects Fred's strategic awareness and initiative.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 15: Fred and George 'fall in on either side of Arthur, wands BLAZING' during the battle. There is no depiction of them having taken on the specific passageway-defense role they volunteered for; they are shown as generic fighters flanking their father rather than executing a distinct strategic assignment.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Fred's proactive volunteering for a specific defensive role — showing tactical initiative and competence — is erased. Instead he becomes one of several anonymous wand-bearers, losing a moment that demonstrates he contributes meaningfully to the battle plan rather than just brawling.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 11 (Great Hall, return to Hogwarts) — Percy reconciliation scene compressed/altered
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 147-154: Fred's reconciliation with Percy is one of his most emotionally significant moments. He calls Percy 'Ministry-loving, family-disowning, power-hungry moron,' then when Percy agrees, Fred extends his hand: 'Well, you can't say fairer than that.' Fred is the one who formally reconciles with Percy — a meaningful act given their estrangement. The exchange is warm and specific, with Fred quoting Percy's own pomposity back at him.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 11: Percy appears alongside Fred and George as they emerge at Hogwarts, but the corpus contains no reconciliation dialogue between Fred and Percy in the film. The reconciliation scene — Fred's specific role in forgiving Percy, the handshake, the 'Ministry-loving, family-disowning, power-hungry moron' exchange — is absent from the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Fred's reconciliation with Percy is a major family relationship moment and one of the few scenes where Fred operates in an emotionally direct rather than comedic register. His formal act of forgiveness (extending his hand after naming Percy's faults) is both funny and genuinely moving. Its absence in the film corpus removes a key dimension of Fred as someone capable of emotional directness and family loyalty beyond jokes, and weakens the tragedy of his subsequent death because the completed arc with Percy is lost.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 16 (Great Hall, aftermath) — Fred's death scene depersonalized
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 164-172: Fred's death follows a specific, deeply characterized sequence: his last words are joy at Percy joking ('You actually are joking, Perce... I don't think I've heard you joke since you were –'), cut off mid-sentence by the explosion. The 'ghost of his last laugh still etched upon his face' is a defining image. Percy shakes his brother, Ron kneels beside them. The scene is witnessed directly by Harry, who cannot comprehend it.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 16: Fred's death is shown entirely from Harry's POV in the Great Hall aftermath — George kneeling over a 'familiar body,' which is then revealed as Fred. The actual moment of death (the corridor explosion, the last laugh, Percy's reaction in the immediate moment) is not present in the film corpus as a witnessed scene. The death is revealed retrospectively in the Great Hall rather than experienced in the corridor.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Fred's death in the book is one of the saga's most devastating moments precisely because of its specific details: the last laugh, the mid-sentence cut-off, the fact that it immediately follows his reconciliation with Percy. The film's choice to reveal the death retrospectively in the Great Hall — as a tableau Harry observes from a distance — removes the witnessed, immediate shock and strips away the specific poetic cruelty of his last laugh. The loss of 'the ghost of his last laugh still etched upon his face' as a visually rendered moment is a significant narrative and emotional damage.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film — Potterwatch broadcast (absent from film corpus)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 111-121: Fred operates as 'Rapier' on Potterwatch, broadcasting calm, witty, strategic commentary about Voldemort to a frightened wizarding world. He is authoritative, funny, and genuinely helpful — distinguishing basilisks from Voldemort, urging people not to panic, signing off with 'safety first.' This is Fred functioning as a resistance leader with real public impact.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The Potterwatch broadcast does not appear in the film corpus at all. Fred's role as a resistance broadcaster — one of his most important contributions to the war effort outside of direct combat — is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Potterwatch is one of Fred's defining moments in Deathly Hallows. It shows him operating independently of Harry's trio, taking real risks, and using his wit in direct service of the resistance. It recontextualizes his humor as a weapon against fear and tyranny — a thematic function that elevates him from comic sidekick to genuine wartime actor. Its complete absence in the film removes a major dimension of Fred's character and his contribution to the wider story.
